It builds on the concept of deferred shading in computer graphics, adapting it to the context of 3D Gaussian Splatting to handle material properties and lighting more effectively [S2, unofficial].

The claim states that the method builds on deferred shading and adapts it to 3D Gaussian Splatting to handle material properties and lighting more effectively. Source [S2] explicitly defines deferred shading as a two-pass technique decoupling geometry from lighting/materials. It further states that recent works have adapted this pipeline to Gaussian Splatting to efficiently render high-frequency, view-dependent effects. Crucially, it notes that performing complex shading calculations on a per-pixel basis (rather than per-Gaussian) 'significantly enhances rendering quality and performance for complex materials.' This directly supports the claim's assertion about handling material properties and lighting more effectively.

The claim states that the final outgoing radiance $L(omega_o)$ is calculated by combining diffuse and specular terms according to the rendering equation $L(omega_o) = int_{Omega} L_i(omega_i) f(omega_i, omega_o) (omega_i cdot mathbf{N}) domega_i$, where $f$ is the BRDF. Source [S1] explicitly provides this exact equation (Eq. 6) and states that 'BRDF consists of both diffuse and specular terms, the integral can also be divided into two parts.' It further details the computation of the diffuse term and the specular term (using GGX and split-sum approximation). Therefore, every fact in the claim is present and supported by the evidence.

Compute Specular Term: Approximate the specular integral using the split-sum approximation: $L_s(\omega_o) \approx \left( \int_{\Omega} f_s(\omega_i, \omega_o) (\omega_i \cdot \mathbf{N}) d\omega_i \right) \cdot \left( \int_{\Omega} L_i(\omega_i) D(\omega_i, \omega_o) (\omega_i \cdot \mathbf{N}) d\omega_i \right)$ [S1, unofficial].

The claim exactly matches the formula provided in Source [S1] (Equation 8) for the split-sum approximation of the specular integral. The source explicitly states: 'Instead, we adopt the split-sum approximation... $L_s(ω_o) ≈ ∫ f_s(ω_i, ω_o) (ω_i · N) dω_i · ∫ L_i(ω_i) D(ω_i, ω_o) (ω_i · N) dω_i$.'
